## 1. The question, frozen

The review answers several questions. The one its title and first sentence make central: **why can no local theory reproduce the predictions of quantum theory?** (Bell's theorem). Range: a Bell experiment — two separated observers, finitely many settings *x, y* and outcomes *a, b*, giving p(ab|xy); extended to *n* parties and arbitrary numbers of settings and outcomes. Kind: "why can it not happen" — something blocks every local route. I hold this fixed. The review's other questions (how to describe, quantify and apply nonlocal correlations; whether the experiments are loophole-free) are separate claims and are not judged here.

## 2. The jobs

J1 (given) why are *a* and *b* correlated at all, with no signal passing? J2 (given) why can no past shared variables λ reproduce the singlet's statistics? J3 (given) why does the failure show in the data alone, with no model of the apparatus? J4 (given) why does the failure not depend on assuming the world is deterministic? J5 (fixed by the authors) the settings are treated as freely chosen, uncorrelated with λ. J6 (added by me) the account must also say why the violation stops at 2√2 and not the algebraic maximum 4. J7 (added) why is this "locality" not quantum field theory's notion?

## 3. The explanation in parts (authors' words)

P1 the locality condition p(ab|xy)=∫dλ q(λ)p(a|x,λ)p(b|y,λ) (Eq. 3). P2 measurement independence, q(λ|x,y)=q(λ). P3 Fine's step: every local behaviour is a mixture of deterministic assignments (Eq. 18). P4 CHSH, S ≤ 2 for every local behaviour (Eq. 4). P5a the state measured is the singlet; P5b the violation tops out at Tsirelson's 2√2 (Eq. 5). P6 the sets nest, local ⊂ quantum ⊂ no-signalling. P7 the "non-communicating PhD students" reading — (3) is exactly what two students with shared classical data can simulate. P8 device-independence. P9 whether every tightest inequality of the local set is broken by some quantum behaviour, in the bipartite case.

## 4. The change list

Covered: turn the measurement directions (S moves); drop the entanglement (no violation); change the numbers of settings and outcomes; swap quantum for an imagined no-signalling box (S = 4); use a different Bell inequality; go from two parties to n. Left out, and said up front: settings correlated with λ (superdeterminism) — assumed away; the field-theory sense of locality — excluded in footnote 1; the interpretive questions — deferred to other reviews; continuous settings — only a few references. Nothing that could have mattered is slipped in later.

## 5. The tests

- **Remove P4.** Other tightest inequalities (I3322, CGLMP, Mermin) still separate the local from the quantum set, so the part doing the work is "some Bell inequality", not CHSH.
- **Swap P5a.** Any nonlocal state does J2, so "it is *this* singlet" is swappable; the shared thing is "a state whose violation reaches the ceiling".
- **Flip.** Could these parts have explained "quantum theory is local"? No — P4 and P5b sit on opposite sides. Passes.
- **Poke.** Change a measurement direction: S moves. Make the state separable: no violation. P1 has both halves.
- **Reverse.** The bound 2 is derived forward from locality, 2√2 forward from the state and the measurements; neither is read back off the result.
- **Hunt the answer in the starting points.** "Nonlocality" is defined negatively by (3), and the paper says plainly that once you accept (3) the theorem is trivial (footnote 3). The spooky connotation is checked by P7 — no signalling.
- **Add J6.** Survives, and it kills the signalling box as an account of *quantum* nonlocality.
- **Best rival:** a local hidden-variable model. The CHSH value tells the two apart, so the theorem is not vacuous.
- **Pull.** P2 against the claim's width: covering superdeterminism costs the free-choice assumption; the paper gives way by narrowing the range and saying so.
- **Patches.** Footnote 1, Section I.C and footnote 3 are stated limits with their reasons inside. No catch-all bin: the open bipartite question (P9) is left open with a citation, not absorbed.
- **Look inside.** The failure needs no model of the workings — that is P8, a feature, not a gap.

| the labels x, y, a, b | loose | conventions; the paper says so |

## 7. Where each part came from

Built in the paper and open to criticism: P1, P3, P4, P5b, P6, P7. Built elsewhere and cited, still criticisable: Tsirelson's bound, the sum-of-squares hierarchies, the enumerations of tightest inequalities, the proof that testing locality is hard. Fixed: P2 — the authors set the free-choice assumption and never test it. Fitted (tuned on past runs): the experimental sections. Asserted: nothing load-bearing.

## 8. What would make it harder to vary

Two things. (a) Give P2 a gauge: state how correlated the settings and λ would have to be to restore a local account, and name a reading that would worry the authors — that turns a "held if" into a "held". (b) Close P9: settle whether every tightest bipartite local inequality is broken by some quantum behaviour. That pins the local/quantum line instead of leaving it where the enumeration stopped.

## 9. What this does not show

Hard to vary is not the same as true. This says the theorem is not a just-so story; it does not say locality is false, does not choose between interpretations of quantum theory, and does not say the experiments were loophole-free — the review's own Section VII.B lists the loopholes. Not looked at: the multipartite, no-signalling and information-theoretic material, which need separate runs.

Write one poke for P2 and run it: generate the settings from a process that cannot have known the source's λ, state beforehand what result would count as a leak from λ to (x, y), then report both halves.
